prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, which brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye. The chair's central question is whether the lattice clock is a distinct invention after the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I think it is, if the citation says what is new: Katori's proposal that atoms trapped in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength have no differential light shift, combined with Lamb-Dicke confinement, so that Doppler and recoil shifts vanish while a very large number of atoms is interrogated at once. A single trapped ion cannot do that, and the comb only counts optical cycles. This is an original idea, demonstrated first in strontium, and then verified in many laboratories (RIKEN, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others) that intercompare their clocks over fibre at the 10^-18 level. That is the experimental verification I require, and I can be 'absolutely sure' of the topic. It opens a door: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of constant variation, relativistic geodesy. On Ye, the citation names invention and realization, and Ye's group is credited for taking the realization to the accuracy and stability frontier with many-body clock physics, not merely for a record. Two names are compact and leave room under the three-person ceiling.
statement.case_against: The unresolved weakness is still novelty and attribution. If the committee concludes that the lattice clock is a better clock built on recognised achievements, we would honour the best later experiment, which I have said we should not do. Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the PTB and NIST groups made real contributions to the early demonstrations and systematic evaluation, and I cannot settle priority dates from memory; an expert report should check this before the vote. Finally, the lattice clock is a gain in precision and not the discovery of an unexpected phenomenon, and Danielsson and Lindroth are right that this differs from IceCube or topological matter. I accept that, but I do not think the mandate restricts the prize to surprises, since an invention that opens a new class of measurements is within it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B008 for a theory-then-experiment story with the broadest opening support, and argues that the 2016 prize covered a different discovery (Thouless-Haldane lineage) from the Z2 classification.
responses.response: I take your distinction seriously, and I do not dispute that the HgTe experiment is verified and the Z2 theory original. I would apply one standard of adjacency to both ballots, as the chair asks: if the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes do not bar the lattice clock because the idea is distinct, then 2016 does not bar B008 for the same reason, and I do not use it against B008. My remaining difficulty is credit, not adjacency. Even with your citation wording around the prediction and the HgTe realization, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the specific HgTe system that Molenkamp measured, and you say you rely on memory for the chronology. For the clock, the two names are the proposer and the leading realizer; for B008, the same test leaves a named gap. That is why B008 stays my first alternative and not my first choice.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube because it found something nature had not announced, the diffuse flux, and argues that B035 is chiefly a gain in precision.
responses.response: I respect the argument that an unexpected discovery is stronger than a refinement, and I agree the diffuse flux is established independently of any source association. I do not think the lattice clock is only a gain in precision: the magic-wavelength concept is a new way to eliminate the dominant systematic errors, and it enabled measurements, such as the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, that no earlier clock could do. Where I differ is on credit. IceCube is a large collaboration, the AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers fall outside the trio, and you concede that trimming Karle cannot be done with a decisive argument. I asked in round 1 who did the original work; for the clock I can answer in two names, for IceCube I cannot yet. I would not block B023, but I cannot support it as a first choice until an expert report settles the roles of Halzen, Karle and Spiering.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B035, citing independent reproduction and the calibration and systematics test as his yardstick, and noted adjacency to B023 through his astroparticle collaborations.
responses.response: I agree that reproduction across independent laboratories with fibre intercomparison is the strongest argument for B035, and it is also why I am comfortable naming only two people. On the pending redefinition of the second, I would not wait for it: it is a consequence the prize enables, not a condition of the discovery. As chair you should record your astroparticle adjacency if B023 advances, as I record my own microscopy adjacency for B019 below. I would also ask that the final citation state the magic-wavelength trapping explicitly, because that wording is what makes the distinction from the comb and ion prizes visible.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B035 with Katori as originator and Ye as the leading realization, and says she normally applies a standard of surprise about nature that favours topological or tunable-matter discoveries.
responses.response: I agree with you that the check on Lemonde and Boyd should be done before the vote and not assumed. On your surprise standard, the lattice clock is not a surprising phenomenon, but cancelling the light shift at a magic wavelength is a non-obvious idea that could have failed on uncontrolled systematics, and the agreement between atomic-structure calculation and experiment that you cite is part of why I trust it. I hold that the Nobel standard asks for an original, verified invention or discovery, not for the largest surprise, and B035 meets that.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B008 because six members proposed the same trio and theory first, experiment second is the pattern the prize has honoured most reliably.
responses.response: The agreement among six members on the trio is real, but agreement on names is not the same as a settled historical record. I would want an expert to state whether the HgTe quantum spin Hall experiment would have been designed without the BHZ proposal. If the answer is no, the trio omits a decisive contributor, and Zhang's death does not make that omission harmless. Your own uncertainty list names this problem and says you might prefer B035 on maturity and attribution over B008 on conceptual novelty. I think the HgTe credit question is not resolved today.

uncertainties: Whether an expert report on priority confirms that Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the PTB and NIST groups do not alter the fair credit to Katori and Ye.
Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice clock as a distinct invention rather than a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which depends on citation wording.
Whether the BHZ prediction for HgTe can be reconciled with the three-person ceiling if the committee turns to B008.
Whether Krivanek and the STEM corrector lineage can be reconciled with a three-person B019 configuration; I do not favour it as a prize today.
Whether the roles of Halzen, Karle and Spiering in IceCube can be established well enough to support B023.
statement.conflict_note: My own field is transmission electron microscopy, so B019 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in my direct research community, and I would recuse myself from any vote on B019 if it advances; I list it only as a distant alternative. As IFSM President I have professional contact with the microscopy community, with no personal tie to Rose, Urban or Haider in my profile. I have no connection to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock community, nor to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or the IceCube founders. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague, relevant only to B004 and B012, which I do not support. Nothing in the round-1 exchange changes my disclosure.
